title: Mumbai Shipping: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A Mumbai shipping borrower owns or charters vessels and converts a fixed asset (a hull) into freight and charter-hire cash. **Cash sits in the vessel, not the balance sheet: value is the charter rate times days on hire, minus voyage costs, crew, insurance and dry-dock.** Capex is lumpy and debt-funded — CSPL relies on debt-funded capex to expand and replace old vessels [11] — so a single vessel purchase can double a small owner's debt. Pricing power is nil on spot; it exists only in term cover. So when a proposal lands, check the charter-backlog months and the rate fixed versus the market rate; if the answer is 'spot', ask for the last twelve months of realised TCE.

## What has changed now
**The local news file is thin: two of the three Mumbai items are the same FICCI conference announcement [1][2], and the only real market signal is a Mumbai owner's MR tanker buying spree [3].** That tells us capital is being deployed into product tankers, not that earnings are safe. The peer read is mixed: Skipper posted record Q2 revenue of Rs 1,384 crores and a Rs 10,066 crores order book, yet flagged elevated shipping freight and export deferrals pushing FY27 growth 1-2% below its 15% target [4][6] — Skipper is an infrastructure/structures maker, not a like-for-like shipping peer, so read it as a freight-cost signal only. Delhivery's record Rs 3,066 crore revenue [5] and Aegis's liquid-segment revenue of INR 178 crore, up 24% [7], are logistics peers, not shipowners. Rating reports are undated: SCI's diversified six-decade track record [10] and JSWIL's ₹2,335 crore free cash with 60-day receivables [9] are healthy but not Mumbai-specific; the Bothra group's ₹197 crore service-tax claims at ~23% of net worth [8] is the cautionary case.

## Where to grow
**Pursue Mumbai MR product-tanker owners with term charters to oil majors, and fleet managers with contracted coastal movement.** Avoid single-vessel spot traders and any group carrying large disputed tax claims — the Bothra case shows how a contingent liability can sit at 23% of net worth [8]. For every new owner, collect from customer: fleet age profile, charter-backlog months, TCE history, and vessel mortgage position.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the hull, not the hope: mortgage the vessel, escrow charter hire, and cap total debt at a level the fixed-hire book services.** Take monthly: charter-hire receipts, days off-hire, dry-dock spend, and a fleet position report. Covenant on minimum charter cover and a debt-service reserve.

## Early-warning signs
- Days off-hire rising two months running (monthly) -> freeze new limits, inspect vessel.
- Charter backlog falling below six months (quarterly) -> move to cash-collateralised structure.
- Dry-dock cost overrun versus budget (per event) -> re-size facility.
- Any new tax or statutory demand above 10% of net worth (quarterly) -> escalate to me.

below six months -> shift to cash-collateralised structure
overrun -> re-size facility and re-test cover
